svg.title: Attention changes which information can influence performance
svg.desc: Two separate experiments. A: Dadds et al. 2006, study 2, boys aged 9 to 17. Three instruction blocks in a fixed order: free viewing, look at eyes, look at mouth, each showing the same illustrative fearful adult face; dashed ovals around the eyes or mouth are editorial markers of the instructed region. Task: identify the emotion; faces shown for 2 s with six response categories. Higher callous-unemotional traits: poorer fear recognition in free viewing, improvement with eye instruction. Fixed order; recognition measured. A 2008 eye-tracking study is separate evidence. B: Newman et al. 2010, adult male prisoners. The participant's eyeblink response to a noise probe is recorded under the eye; a possible shock is delivered to electrodes on two fingers. Red letters signal possible shock and green letters signal no shock in every condition. Uppercase and lowercase examples occur in both colors; color is not tied to letter case. The cue sets are illustrative examples, not a trial sequence. Conditions: threat focus, judge color; other focus with low load, judge letter case; other focus with high load, two-back letter match. Fear-potentiated startle equals threat-trial blink minus no-threat-trial blink. Result: psychopathy-related reduction when threat was outside the task focus; no significant reduction when color was the focus. Recognition, gaze and startle are different measurements; stimulus icons are illustrative.
